newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Oil-rich Kazakhstan to be big world energy player.
newsitem.headline: Oil-rich Kazakhstan to be big world energy player.

text.p: The former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan, sitting on big-league oil and gas reserves, could become a major player on international energy markets, senior government and Western oil officials said on Thursday.
"There are grounds to say you may be able to compare us to Iraq or Kuwait," Kazakh Oil and Gas Minister Nurlan Balgimbayev told an international energy conference in the capital Almaty.

He said that Kazakhstan -- a trail blazer among the former Soviet republics in attracting foreign oil investment dollars while struggling for economic recovery -- had onshore and offshore oil reserves of 24 billion tonnes.
"Kazakhstan will rank within the top tier of the world's energy-producing countries in the next ten to fifteen years," Mobil Oil Kazakhstan Inc President Carl Burnett said.

Officials at Kazakhstan's flagship producing joint venture, Chevron Corp and Mobil Corp's TengizChevroil, said Kazakhstan was well on the road to resolving a major problem -- how to transport crude to markets.

"Cooperation with Russia on pipelines and supplies will be a most important factor in coming years," Balgimbayev said, referring to plans by the multinational Caspian Pipeline Consortium to build a $1.5 billion link from Tengiz to Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.
"The lack of a flexible pipeline system has inhibited growth -- development of the pipeline system is priority number one for Kazakhstan's oil and gas industry."

Western oil executives praised Kazakhstan's privatisation programme, which is unique among those of the former Soviet republics in putting foreign investors in control of most oil and gas enterprises, from production outfits to refineries.
Referring to Almaty's privatisation, Richard Matzke, President of Chevron Overseas Petroleum Inc, said: "It can be cited as a model for all the nations of Central Asia."
Kazakhstan had scored $1.8 billion in foreign oil investment by 1996, with another $40 billion on the negotiating table.
"Negotiating and concluding major hydrocarbons deals around the world is becoming more difficult," Burnett said.
"The opportunities in Kazakhstan compete with the best in the world," he said, adding that Mobil would look at other large projects in Kazakhstan.
Western companies will not be the only ones to share the spoils in Kazakhstan, where oil reserves in its continental shelf of the Caspian are alone 10 billion tonnes.
Balgimbayev said Almaty was in talks with Iran, one of the five states bordering the Caspian and claiming some of its natural resources, on oil deals.
The energy business is not all smooth sailing in this giant, wind-swept country south of Russia, and Western executives complained of red-tape and byzantine rules.
"There continue to be obstacles, especially in the need to simplify regulations and bureaucracy," Matzke said. "But let me make this clear -- the investment climate is improving."
Balgimbayev said the government was working to scrap value added tax on imported oil and gas equipment and to grant tax holidays and other privileges.
The Caspian Sea ranks eighth in the world in terms of discovered reserves, with the sea's Kazakh sector having half that total, or an amount equivalent to that of Western Europe.
The sea has not been fully studied, and may hold even more.
Natural gas reserves may total two trillion cubic metres.

Pierre Bauquis, special advisor to the chairman of French oil company Total SA, said Kazakhstan could be a substantial natural gas supplier to Europe from 2010, when Russian supplies are expected to become less competitive.
